1.d4 d5 2.c4.strategy: Attacks d5 from the wing and offers a pawn that Black cannot keep without conceding something, since White can win it back or gain time. White aims for the bigger centre and lasting pressure on d5; Black usually holds d5 and accepts a cramped game, which it frees with the pawn breaks ...c5 and ...e5.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight to a square from which it covers e5 and d4, without deciding the pawn structure. White keeps every main set-up open and chooses the system once Black has shown a plan, trading the immediate pressure of c4 for flexibility. A quiet, flexible start that often leads into other structures.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4.name: London System
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4.background: Named after the 1922 London tournament, where the opening was played seven times, including in games by Capablanca, Alekhine and Rubinstein. James Mason was the first master-level player to use it regularly, at Vienna 1882, London 1883 and New York 1889.
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4.strategy: Develops the c1 bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 can lock it in, and plans a compact set-up that needs little theory. The set-up makes few demands on Black, who can develop freely, so White gets a low-risk, solid game with little early pressure.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight, puts pressure on d5 and prepares e4, but takes c3 from the c-pawn, so the usual c4 break is not available and d4 loses its natural support. White trades the lasting pressure of the Queen's Gambit for freer piece play.

1.d4 d5 2.Bg5.name: Hodgson Attack
1.d4 d5 2.Bg5.background: Named after the English grandmaster Julian Hodgson, who studied it extensively and found several new ideas; Preston Ware had already tested it in the 1880s. It was a very rare line until the 1980s, when players including Michael Adams and Tony Miles tried it. It is also called the Levitsky Attack, after Stepan Levitsky, and the Pseudo-Trompowsky.
1.d4 d5 2.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, where it attacks e7 and stands ready to answer ...Nf6 with Bxf6, doubling Black's f-pawns. The cost is that b2 is left undefended and the bishop can be harassed by ...h6, so Black gets a solid game with easy development.

1.d4 d5 2.e3.name: Queen's Pawn Game
1.d4 d5 2.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop, heading for a compact set-up with a solid pawn centre. The c1 bishop is shut in behind the pawn, while Black can develop ...Bf5 outside the chain at once. Sound and low-risk, but passive, because nothing is done against d5.

1.d4 d5 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for quick development, hoping to follow up with Nc3 and f3. Theory gives Black several ways to equalise, so the gambit is almost never seen at top level; Black can also simply decline it.

1.d4 d5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which pressures d5 along the long diagonal, in a fianchetto set-up that can add queenside pressure later. Sound but slow: d5 is not challenged yet, so Black can develop without difficulty.

1.d4 d5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which backs up d4 from behind, though the d4-pawn blocks the bishop's view along the long diagonal. Sound but slow: nothing is done against d5, so Black completes development at ease.

1.d4 d5 2.f4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Mason Attack
1.d4 d5 2.f4.strategy: Takes e5 and aims for a compact set-up with a firm pawn wall in the centre. It is playable, but it leaves e4 as a hole for a black knight, opens the e1–h4 diagonal, and makes the c1 bishop a bad bishop behind its own pawns. Black develops easily.

1.d4 d5 2.c3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the d1–a4 diagonal, so an early ...Bf5 can be met by Qb3 against the b7-pawn. The cost is that the b1 knight loses c3 and a later c4 takes a second tempo; Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.a3.strategy: A rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor challenges d5. White's only gain is control of b4, while Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.a4.strategy: Gains a little queenside space but weakens b4, and it neither develops a piece nor challenges d5. Black develops at ease.

1.d4 d5 2.b4.strategy: Gains queenside space but leaves the b4-pawn loose: after ...e6 the f8 bishop attacks it, and ...Bxb4 would come with check, so White must spend a tempo on a3 or c3. Nothing is done about d5 meanwhile.

1.d4 d5 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4, but takes f3 from the g1 knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal to the king. Black can strike at d4 at once with 2...c5, and if White pushes e4 Black can simply take the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.h3.strategy: Stops ...Bg4, but spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that develops nothing and leaves d5 unchallenged. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.h4.strategy: Advances a rook pawn that neither develops a piece nor challenges d5, and loosens the kingside. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Na3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b5 and c4 but does little for the centre. After ...e6 the knight can be exchanged by ...Bxa3 bxa3, which leaves White with doubled a-pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Nd2.strategy: Develops the knight and supports a later e4 or c4, but shuts in the c1 bishop until the knight moves on or b3 is played. Nothing is done against d5, so Black develops easily.

1.d4 d5 2.Nh3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where ...Bxh3 gxh3 gives White doubled h-pawns and a weakened kingside for only the bishop pair. Even without the exchange the knight does little for the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Bd2.strategy: Develops the bishop to a passive square where it takes d2 from the b1 knight, blocks the queen, and does nothing about d5. Black takes the lead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.Be3.strategy: Puts the bishop on the e-pawn's natural square, so e3 is no longer available, and the bishop does nothing about d5. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Qd2.strategy: Brings the queen out early to a square where it blocks the c1 bishop and takes d2 from the b1 knight, and does nothing about d5. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Qd3.name: Amazon Attack
1.d4 d5 2.Qd3.strategy: Brings the queen out before the minor pieces, but ...Bf5 attacks it at once, so White must spend a tempo to move it again. Black gains time and is ahead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.g4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Zurich Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.g4.strategy: Hangs the pawn: 2...Bxg4 wins it, because the queen cannot recapture while the e2-pawn blocks the diagonal, and the kingside is weakened for nothing in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Bh6.strategy: Loses the bishop for nothing, since 2...gxh6 captures it and no White piece defends h6.

1.d4 d5 2.Kd2.strategy: Gives up castling and puts the king on a square where it blocks the c1 bishop and the queen. Black can chase it at once with developing moves.

1.d4 d5.name: Closed Game
1.d4 d5.background: 1.d4 d5 became widely popular by the early 20th century, as players with White began to try first moves other than 1.e4 more often. 1...d5 remains the second most popular reply to 1.d4, after 1...Nf6.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and guards d5 and e4, so Black commits to no pawn structure yet. The knight keeps both a solid set-up and a sharp counter against the undefended b2-pawn available.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5.name: Accelerated London System: Steinitz Countergambit
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5.background: Wilhelm Steinitz played the move against James Mason in the London tournament of 1883. Mason took the pawn, and after 3.dxc5 Nc6 4.Nf3 f6 5.e3 e5 6.Bg3 Bxc5 Black had won it back and taken over the centre; Steinitz won the game.
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and aims to profit from the bishop having left c1: ...Qb6 will press on the undefended b2-pawn before Black has castled. Black offers the c-pawn for quick development and activity, so White usually declines it and keeps two pawns in the centre. The game is sharp, with counterplay for Black.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 e6.strategy: Supports d5 in the manner of the Queen's Gambit Declined and opens the f8-bishop's path to d6, where it can challenge White's bishop. The cost is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in and which often struggles to find a good square. The game is solid and strategic.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c6.strategy: Supports d5 in Slav style and keeps the c8-bishop free to come out to f5, while the queen gains b6 against the undefended b2-pawn. The c6-pawn takes that square from the b8-knight, but the set-up is solid and leads to a calm, strategic game.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bf5.background: The Göttingen manuscript, the earliest known work devoted entirely to modern chess, already includes 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bf5 among its twelve openings; the possible dates given for it are 1500–1505 and 1471. Jacob Sarratt's “A Treatise on the Game of Chess” (1808) gives the line as well, continuing 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.f3.
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bf5.strategy: Mirrors White's development and brings the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in. The symmetrical structure is sound but offers Black few winning chances, and without a transposition the game tends toward a quiet draw. White's most testing plan is to steer into a Queen's Gambit with c4.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on d4 and prepares to bring out the c8-bishop actively and to strike later with ...e5. It blocks the c-pawn, so it can no longer support the centre, and d4 is easy for White to keep guarded.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nd7.strategy: Develops the knight to a square from which it supports ...e5 and ...c5 and leaves the c-pawn free to support the centre. It blocks the c8-bishop and the queen's file, so Black is slightly cramped, and White can build the usual London set-up undisturbed.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bg4.strategy: Pins the e2-pawn against the queen, so 3.e3 is ruled out for now: 3...Bxd1 would follow. White can simply develop, or question the bishop at once.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but with the pawn already on d5 the bishop bites on its own pawn for the time being. The move develops nothing yet and loosens c6, so White can build the usual London set-up at leisure.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the kingside bishop, which then presses on d4 along the long diagonal. It is sound but slow, and White meets it with the usual London set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 h5.strategy: An uncommon sideline with a trap: the routine 3.e3? closes the bishop's retreat to d2, and 3...e5! lets Black trap it with ...f6, ...g5 and ...h4 and win it for pawns. White avoids this by keeping the retreat open, for example with a developing knight move, after which the h-pawn does little for Black.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it aims at b4 and c5 but takes little part in the fight for the centre. It does guard c7, yet costs time that White uses to build the usual London set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bd7.strategy: Puts the bishop on a passive square, where it takes d7 from the b8-knight and blocks the queen's d-file. It does less than ...Bf5 would, and White simply goes on developing.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Be6.strategy: Puts the bishop on e6, where it blocks the e-pawn and with it the f8-bishop, so the usual plan of freeing that bishop is gone. White develops at leisure while the bishop does little.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where it blocks the c8-bishop and the knight and can be hit with tempo by a White knight. Black spends time on the queen instead of developing.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 or g4 but offers the trade 3.Bxh6 gxh6, after which the doubled, isolated h-pawns are a lasting weakness in Black's kingside.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank move that only prepares ...b5. It develops no piece and leaves the centre alone, so White develops unhindered.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn advance that takes b4 but develops nothing and does not contest the centre. White develops and gains space at leisure.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 b5.strategy: Pushes the b-pawn without developing a piece, weakens c5 and c6 and makes the pawn a target: after 3.e3 the f1-bishop threatens Bxb5+, and a4 can attack it too. Black then spends further moves to hold it.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 f6.strategy: Aims for ...e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal, so once White has played e3 the queen can check on h5. Black spends a tempo without developing a piece, while White simply develops.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 f5.strategy: Aims for a solid wall of pawns on f5, e6 and d5, but weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal and leaves e5 as a permanent hole, which the f4-bishop already controls and a knight can occupy from f3. Once the wall stands, the c8-bishop is hemmed in behind its own pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that develops nothing; its point, a later ...g5 against the f4-bishop, would loosen Black's own kingside. White simply develops, and h3 gives the bishop a retreat on h2.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bh3.strategy: Gives up the bishop for nothing: 3.Nxh3 or 3.gxh3 wins it, and Black has no compensation for the piece.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Qd6.strategy: Puts the queen where the f4-bishop takes it: 3.Bxd6 wins the queen, and after the recapture Black has only a bishop in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and puts the king in front of the queen and the c8-bishop, blocking both. After 3.e3 the f1-bishop can already check on b5, and the king stays exposed in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 e5.strategy: Offers a pawn that 3.Bxe5 simply wins: the bishop can retreat when attacked, d4 stays guarded by the queen, and Black has opened the position but has no compensation for the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn: 3.Bxg5 wins it, because the queen cannot recapture with the e7-pawn in the way, and the bishop remains active. The advance also weakens the kingside for nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.e4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Accelerated London System, Steinitz Countergambit, Morris Countergambit
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.e4.strategy: Gives up the e-pawn so that d5 follows and cramps Black's pieces. It is a gambit for space: White is a pawn down and needs the cramp to be worth it.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.dxc5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Accelerated London System, Steinitz Countergambit Accepted
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.dxc5.strategy: Wins a pawn that does not stay won: the capture gives up White's central d-pawn, and Black regains the pawn easily and takes over the centre. White has swapped the centre for a pawn that is soon lost again.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.e3.strategy: Supports the d4 pawn so that it no longer depends on the queen, and opens the f1-bishop; the c1-bishop is already outside the chain, so nothing is shut in. White declines the c5 pawn to keep a sturdy centre, and accepts that Black's queen can pressure b2, which no piece guards.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.e4 dxe4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Accelerated London System, Steinitz Countergambit, Morris Countergambit Accepted
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.e4 dxe4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn and attacks the d4 pawn a second time with the queen, so White must react at once. Black keeps the extra material for now and has to finish development carefully, since White's gambit is played for open lines.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.e4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the d-pawn, and the e4 pawn is still attacked by the d5 pawn, so White has to spend time regaining material. Recapturing with the queen on d4 walks into ...Nc6 with a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5 3.e4 Nc6.strategy: Adds a second attacker on the d4 pawn with a developing move instead of taking a pawn. It keeps the tension, but White chooses how to resolve it, and Black may end up winning only one of the pawns on offer.

1.d4 d5 2.Bg5 Bg4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Levitsky Attack, Welling Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Bg5 Bg4.strategy: Answers the bishop with the same move: each bishop now looks at the other side's e-pawn with the queen behind it. The symmetry is shallow, since White moves first and decides when and how it is broken, so Black gains nothing from copying.

1.d4 d5 2.Bg5 h6.strategy: Asks the bishop what it wants at once: it must retreat from the attack on e7. Black accepts a slow kingside pawn move in return for a solid set-up, and will pressure b2, which the bishop has left undefended.

1.d4 d5 2.Bg5 c6.strategy: A solid reply that supports d5 and makes room for the queen to pressure b2, which the bishop has left undefended. Black ignores the bishop for now and relies on a compact structure.

1.d4 d5 2.Bg5 Nf6.strategy: Falls in with White's idea: the bishop takes the knight and Black recaptures with doubled f-pawns, a weakened structure in return for the bishop pair and open lines. Playable, but White has chosen the structure.

1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6.name: Queen's Pawn Game
1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it controls e4. White's e3 has shut in the bishop on c1 for the moment, so Black can simply develop and see what set-up White chooses, with a solid pawn on d5 and nothing to fear.

1.d4 d5 2.e3 e6.strategy: Backs d5 with the e-pawn and opens the way for the kingside pieces, a solid set-up with a firm centre. The cost is the light-squared bishop, which stays shut in behind its own pawns until Black finds a way to free it.

1.d4 d5 2.e3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before it can be shut in, and eyes the e4 square. A sound and active alternative against White's quiet set-up, though the bishop may be chased or traded before the rest of Black's pieces are out.

1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Bd3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Stonewall Attack
1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Bd3.background: The Stonewall Attack became established in master play after Harry Nelson Pillsbury won all six games in which he used it at the two New York tournaments of 1893. It began to disappear from top-level chess by the early 1920s but remains a popular choice at club level.
1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active diagonal, aiming at h7, and builds a compact pawn chain, with a later f4 to control e5 and prepare a kingside attack. The price is an inflexible structure, weak light squares and a c1-bishop shut in behind its own pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps White's options open: a compact set-up with the centre pawns on d4 and e3 and a well-timed e4 as the aim, or a later c4 to challenge d5. Solid rather than ambitious, it gives White a safe position and Black no targets.

1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once and reaches the structures of the Queen's Gambit with e3 already played. The pressure on the centre is real, but the c1-bishop is shut in behind the e-pawn, and Black can either take the pawn or simply hold d5.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and takes space on the queenside. White's h-pawn move has done nothing for the centre or for development, so Black can strike at the centre first and the d4 pawn has to be defended.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and watches e4. White's h-pawn move has done nothing for the centre or development, so Black can develop freely and keep every set-up open.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 Bf5.strategy: Brings the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain at once, before it can be shut in. Sound and active, but it commits a piece before Black knows what set-up White chooses.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move, defending d4. But Black can exchange on d4 and leave White without a central pawn, and the h-pawn move has still brought nothing. Playable, but White has spent a tempo for no gain.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.e4.name: Kádas Opening: Myers Variation
1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.e4.strategy: A pawn gambit that opens the centre at once. But the pawn on e4 is attacked by the d-pawn and d4 by the c-pawn, and the h-pawn move has done nothing for development, so Black can take a pawn and simply develop.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.c3.strategy: Defends d4 with a pawn, so the knight is not tied to it and the centre holds. It cannot give back the tempo lost on h4, but it is the sound way to reach an ordinary queen's-pawn game.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.e3.strategy: Defends d4 and frees the f1-bishop and the queen, a patient set-up. If Black captures on d4, White recaptures with a pawn and keeps a central pawn, but the c1-bishop is shut in for now.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and leaves White without a pawn on the central squares while Black keeps its pawn on d5. White recaptures easily, but the exchange opens the c-file for Black and White's h-pawn push has still brought nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks d4 a second time. Black adds to the pressure on the d4 pawn and keeps the capture in reserve, while White's h-pawn move still gives nothing to the position.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and adds control of e4 without clarifying the centre. Sound, but it allows White a bishop to g5 that hits the knight, and a trade there damages Black's pawn structure.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.c3.name: Kádas Opening: Kádas Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.c3.strategy: Declines the simple recapture and offers a pawn to open lines for quick development. But the sacrifice has to be earned: Black can accept it and, with an extra pawn, simply develop while White's h4 push does nothing for the attack.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Recaptures and centralises the knight. White has lost its central pawn but is developed, and the position is level. Black can gain space with a pawn push at the knight, and the h4 move has still brought nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which comes out early: ...Nc6 attacks it at once and Black develops with a gain of time. Playable, since the queen has safe squares, but White has nothing to show for the h-pawn move.
